meta.title: Who really said "Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Douglas Adams. Scott Adams wrote it in The Dilbert Principle (1996), page 324. A 2013 Fast Company article swapped the surname.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to Scott Adams, The Dilbert Principle (1996), p. 324. The Douglas Adams credit began with a 2013 Fast Company mix-up.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — actually Scott Adams
answer.sourceLine: Scott Adams — the Dilbert cartoonist, no relation to the Hitchhiker’s Guide author — wrote the line in The Dilbert Principle (HarperBusiness, 1996), introducing it in the book’s final chapter with the words “I have a saying.” Quote Investigator verified it on paper at quote page 324 ↗, and traced the Douglas Adams credit to a single reporter’s surname mix-up in 2013.

source.heading: The Dilbert Principle, final chapter

docMeta.dd: Quote page 324, in the book’s final chapter

source.excerpt:
Finally—and this is the last time I’m going to say it—we’re all idiots and we’re going to make mistakes. That’s not necessarily bad. I have a saying: “Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep.”

Keep your people fresh, happy, and efficient. Set a target, then get out of the way. Let art happen. Sometimes idiots can accomplish wonderful things.
trail: 1996 — Scott Adams publishes The Dilbert Principle (HarperBusiness, New York). In the final chapter he writes “I have a saying” and gives the line. Quote Investigator records the citation at quote page 324, verified on paper ↗.
Independently listed — Wikiquote files the sentence under The Dilbert Principle (1996) ↗, keeping Adams’s “I have a saying” introduction intact.
5 October 2011 — Ricky Gervais quotes the line in Wired UK and names Scott Adams as its author ↗.
15 July 2013 — a Fast Company profile of Gervais by Drake Baer reassigns the words to Douglas Adams ↗. Quote Investigator identifies this as the source of the confusion.

author.name: Scott Adams
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1957–2026 · American cartoonist and author, creator of Dilbert
author.bio: Scott Raymond Adams (8 June 1957 – 13 January 2026) was an American cartoonist and satirist, best known for Dilbert, the comic strip about cubicle life he launched in 1989. The Dilbert Principle (1996) was his first business book — a bestseller that spent months on the New York Times list — and it carried the strip’s satire of management into prose. The creativity line sits in its closing chapter, the one place in the book where Adams drops the joke voice and offers advice he actually means; he prefaces it with “I have a saying”, which is about as clear an authorship claim as a quotation ever comes with.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Most quotation sites do get this one right and file it under Scott Adams. But three other names are attached to it, and one of them has a precisely datable origin.

items.why: A Fast Company profile of Ricky Gervais by Drake Baer, published 15 July 2013, introduced the line as coming from “Hitchhikers’ Guide to the Galaxy author Douglas Adams ↗.” Douglas Adams had died in 2001, and the words appear in none of his work. Quote Investigator attributes the error to the shared surname.
Gervais used the line in an article for Wired UK on 5 October 2011, writing “In fact Scott Adams said… ↗” He named the right man; the credit was lost downstream of him, not by him.
A Goodreads quotation page ↗ files the line under Adam Grant and his book Originals. Goodreads labels such entries as added by its community and not verified by the site.

misattribution.truthLine: Scott Adams wrote it, in the final chapter of The Dilbert Principle (1996), quote page 324 ↗, and presented it as his own saying.

context.heading: How one surname moved a quote
lead: The line closes a chapter of jokes with a piece of advice Adams evidently meant. Having spent The Dilbert Principle arguing that the least competent people get promoted, he ends by conceding the obvious — “we’re all idiots and we’re going to make mistakes” — and then reframes that as the working condition of anyone who makes things. The aphorism is the reframe.

What moved it was not a forger but a footnote. Ricky Gervais quoted the line in Wired UK in October 2011 and credited Scott Adams by name. When Gervais made the same point to a Fast Company reporter two years later, the credit arrived as “Adams” and left as the wrong one: the piece introduced it as coming from “another sagastic, jesterly Brit,” the Hitchhiker’s Guide author. A cartoonist from California became an English novelist in the space of a clause.
context.detailsSummary: Why the swap was so easy to make
detailsBody: Douglas Adams is one of the internet’s strongest attractors for clever, warm, slightly rueful lines — the tone of this one fits him well enough that nobody stopped to check. He also happens to share a surname with a writer who published aphorisms about creative work in the same decade.

Notably, the correct credit largely held: most quotation sites still carry the line under Scott Adams. The Douglas Adams version is a real and traceable stream rather than the dominant one — which is unusual, and worth saying plainly instead of overstating the confusion.
context.pull: “I have a saying” — the four words that settle the question.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the saying should be ascribed to Scott Adams, cites it to The Dilbert Principle (HarperBusiness, New York, 1996) at quote page 324 marked 'Verified on paper', quotes the surrounding passage beginning 'Finally—and this is the last time I'm going to say it', and attributes the Douglas Adams credit to a July 2013 Fast Company article by Drake Baer caused by the shared surname.

Wikiquote's Scott Adams page lists 'I have a saying: "Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep."' under the section heading for The Dilbert Principle (1996), and gives Adams's dates as 8 June 1957 – 13 January 2026.

The archived 18 July 2013 capture of Drake Baer's Fast Company article (bylined 'By: Drake Baer', dated July 15, 2013) states that the line comes from 'Hitchhikers' Guide to the Galaxy author Douglas Adams, who said that "creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep."'

The archived 6 October 2011 capture of Ricky Gervais's Wired UK article, titled "'I may have been wrong about Twitter', writes Ricky Gervais", contains the sentence 'In fact Scott Adams said, "Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep."'
Wikipedia gives Scott Adams's birth date as June 8, 1957 and death date as January 13, 2026, and describes him as an American cartoonist, author and commentator best known as the creator of Dilbert.

Wikipedia's article on The Dilbert Principle covers the 1996 book by Scott Adams published by HarperBusiness, noting it sold more than a million copies and spent 43 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list.
Wikipedia gives Douglas Adams's dates as 11 March 1952 – 11 May 2001 and describes him as an English author, humourist and screenwriter best known for The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

A Goodreads quotation page attributes 'Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep.' to Adam Grant and his book Originals: How Non-conformists Change the World, with Goodreads' standard notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified by Goodreads.
The Internet Archive holds a digitised, borrowable copy of the 1996 edition of The Dilbert Principle by Scott Adams.
